title: Yishtabach
hookLine: the closing blessing of the verses of song

lines: ENDINGS SAY WHAT IT WAS ABOUT.
cards: Every good piece of music knows how to end. The last chord of a symphony. The final chorus everyone sings.
Even a playlist has a last song picked on purpose. Endings tell you what the whole thing was about.
The verses of song have been building: the blessing for the one who spoke, David's thanks, the alphabet psalm, five hallelujahs, the sea. Then they close with a single paragraph. It adds no new idea.
It gathers every word for praise it can find and stacks them, like a final chord.

teach.h: MAY YOUR NAME BE PRAISED FOREVER.
teach.b: It's called Yishtabach, from its first word: yishtabach shimcha la'ad malkeinu, may your name be praised forever, our king. Then the stack.

To you belong song and praise, hallel and hymn, strength and dominion, victory, greatness and might, praise and glory, holiness and sovereignty, blessings and thanksgivings. Count them and you get fifteen.
Commentators have connected that number to the fifteen Songs of Ascents in the Psalms, and to the fifteen steps in the Temple where, the Mishnah says, the Levites stood and sang. Notice the form.
Most blessings start with baruch, blessed. Yishtabach doesn't, because it isn't a separate blessing. It's the closing half of Baruch She'amar, the blessing that opened the verses of song.
The two are bookends around everything in between, and the custom is not to talk between them. Look at the opening words in Hebrew, too.

The first letters of shimcha, la'ad, malkeinu and ha'el spell Shlomo, Solomon, and a tradition credits him with the prayer. That may be a later reading, but it shows how closely people have looked at every word.
And the very last phrase calls God habocher b'shirei zimrah: the one who chooses songs of praise.
Not the one who demands them. The one who chooses them, as if, out of everything in the world, the songs people sing are something God picks out and wants.

how: Yishtabach closes the verses of song every morning, often said standing; it is followed by half Kaddish and the call to prayer, Barchu, which opens the Shema and its blessings.

games.q: you're closing a long morning of songs. what do you add?
o: every word for praise you can find, stacked together.
a request for the day ahead.
games.why: Yishtabach adds no new idea. it stacks fifteen words of praise, like a final chord, and calls God the one who chooses songs.

practice: Think of the last thing you finished, a meal, a shift, this lesson, and before moving on, give it an ending. Stack the good things in it, the way Yishtabach stacks its words: it was warm, it was useful, someone laughed, it's done.
If you pray, you can close with yishtabach shimcha la'ad, may your name be praised forever.
